newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong shares hit another record, Tokyo on rise.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong shares hit another record, Tokyo on rise.

text.p: Hong Kong shares notched a record closing high for the third consecutive day on Wednesday and Tokyo's key Nikkei index added more than one percent, inspired by a surging Wall Street.

Most Asian markets gained ground, with Sydney and Singapore recording the healthiest gains and Taipei hitting a 22-month high. But in Bombay poor company results stripped 2.43 percent off the benchmark index.
Brokers said Hong Kong's Hang Seng index, which rose 110.23 points, or 0.84 percent, to its record close of 13,167.16 was boosted by a positive outlook for lending rates.
The index earlier set a new intraday high of 13,229.15.

"We haven't seen any visible signs of inflation, any sign of a rise in interest rates," said Gary Wong, sales director at Vickers Ballas. "In the U.S., Hong Kong and China everything seems to be going our way."
"The market is up on the long bond and liquidity," said Wong.

The yield on the U.S. 30-year treasury bond has continued to trend at low levels, closing Tuesday trading in New York down at 6.44 percent, compared with 6.47 percent at Monday's close, and pointing to continued low, steady interest rates till 1997, brokers said.

Tokyo's Nikkei ended 233.78 points, or 1.12 percent, higher at 21,189.96 after domestic and institutional investors bought blue-chip issues, brokers said. They said Wall Street's 50-point rise to a record high close of 6,397 buoyed the market.
"Blue chips led the way today," said Yasuo Ueki, general manager at Nikko Securities.
"Foreign investors were net buyers and they led the market higher, brightening sentiment on the whole," Seiki Orimi, an analyst at Dai-ichi Securities, said.
Taiwan share prices ended up 41.48 points, or 0.62 percent, to 6,729.36, its highest close since January 11, 1995.

Brokers said the upward momentum was fuelled in part by what brokers called politically motivated, state-linked buying marking six months since President Lee Teng-hui's inauguration. Lee, a landslide victor in March in Taiwan's first direct presidential election, was sworn in on May 20 and urged state agencies at the time to boost investment in six months.
Thai stocks made slight gains at the close in a dull afternoon session governed by a lack of further developments following the weekend's general election, traders said.
The SET Index closed at 966.43, up 2.24 points, or 0.23 percent on the day.
"The amount of action was very limited... I think it was just waiting for some news to do something different," said Richard Henderson, head of research at Krungthai Thanakit.
Australian shares raced to a record close as an afternoon rally pushed an already Dow-inspired market to higher territory.
The All Ordinaries index rose 26.70 points, or 1.13 percent, to 2,392.7.
Singapore share prices closed higher on the back of Wall Street, positive non-oil domestic export figures and Hong Kong's new high, dealers said.
The Straits Times Industrials Index closed up 24.10 points, or 1.11 percent, at 2,194.28.
In Bombay, traders said disappointing first-half profit announcements sent shares prices reeling.
The Bombay Stock Exchange's index crashed 76.22 points to a provisional 3,063.11 close.
Jakarta's Composite Index fell 8.45 points, or 1.37 percent, to close at 606.76 points.
At 11.39 GMT, the dollar traded at 111.18/1.23 yen and 1.4996/03 marks.
Hong Kong gold prices rose to end at $378.25/75 an ounce against Tuesday's New York close of $377.85/378.25.
SIMEX Brent crude futures rallied, the prompt January contract last trading at $23.50 per barrel, up 12 cents from London's close.
